title: The 2025 Guide to Cloud FinOps
desc: Strategies for controlling cloud spend in an era of AI adoption.
author: James Lau
keyTakeaways: AI workloads can inflate cloud bills by 3–5× if not governed from day one
Tagging hygiene and showback reports drive accountability at team level
Reserved Instances and Savings Plans typically yield 30–50% savings vs on-demand
FinOps is not just a cost exercise — it unlocks speed by removing financial friction

sections.heading: Why FinOps Has Never Mattered More
body: Enterprise cloud spend surpassed $600 billion globally in 2024, and analyst firms project it will cross $1 trillion by 2028. AI workloads are the primary driver of this acceleration — GPU-backed compute is orders of magnitude more expensive than general-purpose instances, and development teams are spinning up experiments faster than finance teams can track them.

Without a structured FinOps practice, organisations are flying blind. Bills arrive at month-end, engineering teams have no feedback loop on cost, and platform owners are left scrambling to explain variance. The answer is not budget cuts — it is real-time visibility, shared accountability, and a culture that treats cloud spend as a first-class engineering metric.

sections.heading: The Three Pillars of Mature FinOps
body: A sustainable FinOps programme rests on three interlocking capabilities:
bullets: Visibility: Granular cost allocation using resource tags, linked accounts, and cost anomaly detection. Every dollar must be attributable to a team, product, or project.
Accountability: Showback and chargeback models that surface unit economics to engineering managers in real time — not in a quarterly spreadsheet.
Optimisation: A continuous improvement cycle covering right-sizing, commitment discounts (Reserved Instances, Savings Plans, CUDs), and architectural refactoring to eliminate waste.

sections.heading: Governing AI and GPU Spend
body: The most common FinOps failure mode in 2025 is the runaway AI experiment. A data science team provisions a p4d.24xlarge instance for model training, forgets to terminate it over a weekend, and returns on Monday to a $14,000 surprise.

Effective AI spend governance requires: automated instance scheduler policies, budget alerts with hard stops, a centralised ML platform team that brokers GPU access, and per-project cost attribution from the moment a notebook is launched.

sections.heading: Commitment Strategies That Actually Work
body: Reserved Instances and Savings Plans remain the highest-leverage cost lever available, yet many enterprises are under-committed because finance and engineering cannot agree on a baseline. The best practice is to commit on the stable, predictable baseline at the account or organisation level, and leave variable burst capacity on-demand.

Cloudyo's benchmark data shows that enterprises with mature commitment coverage (>60% of spend on commitments) achieve an average effective discount of 38% versus on-demand equivalents. For a $5M annual cloud bill, that represents $1.9M in recoverable savings.

sections.heading: Building a FinOps Centre of Excellence
body: A FinOps Centre of Excellence (CoE) does not need to be large — three to five dedicated practitioners embedded across engineering, finance, and architecture can transform an organisation's cost posture within a quarter.

The CoE's mandate is to establish standards (tagging policy, commitment review cadence, anomaly response SLA), build tooling integrations (cloud cost platforms, Slack alerting, Jira tickets for waste), and run monthly allocation reviews with each product team.

title: Financial Services: $12M Saved on Oracle Renewal
desc: How our procurement experts secured landmark savings for a global bank.
author: Rachel Ng
keyTakeaways: $12M in savings secured across a 3-year Oracle enterprise agreement
Audit exposure eliminated before contract signature
Cloudyo's ex-Oracle advisors brought insider pricing intelligence to the table
Deal completed 6 weeks ahead of the bank's renewal deadline

sections.heading: Client Background
body: Our client is a Tier-1 bank headquartered in Asia Pacific, with operations across 18 markets and an Oracle estate spanning database, middleware, and ERP. With approximately 12,000 Oracle processor licences in deployment, the annual maintenance bill alone exceeded $8M.

The bank's IT leadership had managed Oracle renewals internally for over a decade — a process that had served them adequately when the estate was static. By 2024, a combination of cloud migrations, M&A activity, and virtualisation projects had created significant compliance uncertainty.

sections.heading: The Challenge
body: Six months before the enterprise agreement renewal date, Oracle's licence compliance team initiated a pre-renewal audit. The timing was not coincidental — Oracle regularly uses audit leverage to reset commercial conversations on more favourable terms.

The bank's internal team identified three areas of potential exposure: uncounted processor cores in a virtualised environment, database options deployed beyond their licensed footprint, and a recent acquisition that had brought additional Oracle installations into scope without corresponding licences.

sections.heading: How Cloudyo Engaged
body: Cloudyo was engaged on a success-fee basis, with our procurement advisory team taking full ownership of the Oracle relationship. Our team included two former Oracle licence compliance managers who understood the audit methodology from the inside.

Over eight weeks, we conducted an independent licence position analysis, identified defensible positions in the virtualisation findings, and prepared a detailed compliance response that reduced the bank's stated exposure by 71% before negotiations commenced.

sections.heading: Negotiation Strategy and Outcome
body: Armed with accurate licence data, a clear understanding of Oracle's discount authority structure, and proprietary benchmark data on comparable deals, Cloudyo led a structured negotiation across three rounds. We introduced competitive alternatives — including open-source database migration paths — to create genuine leverage.

The final agreement delivered $12M in savings over three years versus Oracle's opening position, eliminated the audit risk entirely through a contractual clean-up clause, and secured a price lock protecting against Oracle's annual maintenance uplift for the duration of the term.

sections.heading: What Made the Difference
body: The bank's previous renewal had been conducted without independent advice. The single most important factor in this engagement was the quality of the licence position analysis — knowing exactly what you own and what you use is the foundation of any successful negotiation.

Oracle's commercial teams are highly trained and negotiate hundreds of enterprise deals each year. Bringing advisors who have operated on that side of the table is not just an advantage — in deals of this complexity, it is essential.

title: Building AI-Ready Data Architecture
desc: A technical blueprint for modernizing enterprise data platforms.
author: Wei Chen
authorRole: Head of Data & AI Practice, Cloudyo
keyTakeaways: Most enterprises are not AI-blocked by model capability — they are blocked by data quality and accessibility
The data lakehouse pattern unifies batch and streaming data for ML workloads at scale
Data mesh principles enable domain ownership without sacrificing governance
Vector databases and semantic search are now core infrastructure requirements for GenAI

sections.heading: Why Most AI Projects Fail Before They Start
body: Industry surveys consistently show that fewer than 20% of enterprise AI pilots reach production. The bottleneck is rarely the model — foundation models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and others have made advanced AI capability broadly accessible. The bottleneck is data.

Siloed data warehouses, inconsistent schemas, undocumented pipelines, and poor data quality create a tax on every AI initiative. Data scientists spend 60–80% of their time on data preparation rather than model development. Solving this requires architectural investment, not more data science headcount.

sections.heading: The Lakehouse: A Unified Foundation
body: The data lakehouse pattern, pioneered by Databricks and now supported across all major cloud providers, combines the low-cost storage flexibility of a data lake with the query performance and ACID guarantees of a data warehouse.

For AI workloads specifically, the lakehouse provides a unified storage tier for both structured data (used in traditional analytics) and unstructured data (documents, images, audio — the raw material for LLM fine-tuning and RAG applications). Open table formats such as Apache Iceberg and Delta Lake are the recommended standards for enterprise deployments.

sections.heading: Data Mesh and Domain Ownership
body: As organisations scale, centralised data engineering teams become bottlenecks. The data mesh paradigm distributes data ownership to domain teams — customer, product, finance, operations — each of which owns, publishes, and maintains its own data products.

A federated governance layer provides the guardrails: shared schemas for cross-domain joins, unified access control policies, and a data catalogue that makes assets discoverable. Platform engineering teams provide the infrastructure toolkit (pipelines, quality checks, cataloguing) as a self-service capability.

sections.heading: Vector Databases: The GenAI Infrastructure Layer
body: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as the dominant pattern for grounding LLM responses in enterprise knowledge bases. RAG requires a vector database — a specialised store that indexes high-dimensional embeddings and supports semantic similarity search at scale.

Production deployments should evaluate Pinecone, Weaviate, Milvus, and the native vector search capabilities built into PostgreSQL (pgvector) and the major cloud data platforms. Selection criteria include latency requirements, scale, hybrid search capability (dense + sparse), and integration with existing data infrastructure.

sections.heading: MLOps: Industrialising Model Delivery
body: A model that exists only in a notebook has zero business value. MLOps is the practice of applying DevOps principles to machine learning — continuous training, automated testing, reproducible experiments, and monitored production deployments.

A minimal viable MLOps stack for an enterprise includes: an experiment tracking platform (MLflow, Weights & Biases), a feature store for consistent feature serving across training and inference, a model registry with versioning and approval workflows, and a monitoring layer that detects data drift and model degradation in production.

sections.heading: A Practical Roadmap
body: Cloudyo recommends a three-phase approach for enterprises building AI-ready data infrastructure:
bullets: Phase 1 — Foundation (0–6 months): Inventory existing data assets, establish a lakehouse landing zone, implement a data catalogue, define tagging and governance standards.
Phase 2 — Enablement (6–12 months): Migrate priority data domains to lakehouse, deploy a feature store, launch an internal data marketplace, establish MLOps toolchain.

Phase 3 — Scale (12–24 months): Expand to all data domains via mesh operating model, build RAG infrastructure for GenAI use cases, implement continuous monitoring and cost governance for ML workloads.

title: Understanding Microsoft's New Commerce Experience
desc: What the latest changes mean for your enterprise agreement.
author: Sarah Kim
keyTakeaways: NCE locks most subscriptions into annual terms — monthly flexibility carries a 20% premium
EA customers are not directly affected but face pressure to migrate to MCA
Price protection during the term is a genuine benefit, but renewal uplift risk remains
Proactive licence optimisation before renewal is more important than ever under NCE

sections.heading: What Is the New Commerce Experience?
body: Microsoft's New Commerce Experience (NCE) is a significant restructuring of how Microsoft 365, Azure, Dynamics 365, and Power Platform subscriptions are purchased through the Cloud Solution Provider (CSP) channel. Introduced in 2022 and progressively mandated, NCE changes term structures, cancellation policies, and pricing rules in ways that have significant commercial implications for enterprise customers.

The core change is the introduction of committed annual or multi-year subscription terms, replacing the previous month-to-month flexibility that many organisations relied on. Under NCE, monthly subscriptions are available but carry a 20% price premium over the annual equivalent — a deliberate commercial nudge toward commitment.

sections.heading: What Changed for CSP Customers
body: Under the legacy CSP model, resellers could provision and cancel Microsoft 365 licences on a monthly basis with minimal notice. This was popular with organisations managing seasonal workforce fluctuations or post-acquisition integrations. NCE removes this flexibility for standard commercial customers.

Annual subscriptions under NCE can be cancelled within the first 72 hours of a term or billing anniversary. After that window, the customer is committed for the remainder of the annual term. Mid-term seat reductions are not permitted — though seat additions are allowed and billed pro-rata.

sections.heading: Impact on Enterprise Agreement Customers
body: Enterprise Agreement (EA) customers are not directly subject to NCE rules — the EA is a separate commercial vehicle that still offers the familiar True-Up model and three-year term structure. However, Microsoft is actively promoting the Microsoft Customer Agreement (MCA) as the successor to the EA, and MCA subscriptions are governed by NCE terms.

Organisations approaching EA renewal should carefully evaluate whether migrating to MCA makes sense for their situation. The MCA offers more granular billing and faster provisioning, but loses some of the price certainty and negotiation leverage available under a fully negotiated EA.

sections.heading: The Seat Optimisation Imperative
body: One of the most common errors we see at clients is carrying excess Microsoft 365 licences that cannot be reduced mid-term. Under legacy CSP, surplus licences could be cancelled on 30 days' notice — a safety valve that no longer exists under NCE annual terms.

Before your next renewal cycle, we recommend conducting a full utilisation review: active users vs assigned licences, feature usage across licence tiers, and opportunities to downgrade users from E5 to E3 or E1 where functionality usage does not justify the premium tier. For a 1,000-seat organisation, moving 200 users from E5 to E3 saves approximately $90,000 per year at list price.

sections.heading: Negotiating Under NCE
body: Despite the standardisation of NCE, there remains meaningful room to negotiate — particularly for organisations purchasing at scale through an EA or a large CSP transaction. Cloudyo has secured price concessions of 15–25% below list on Microsoft 365 E3/E5 for clients with 500+ seats by combining volume leverage with competitive alternatives and Microsoft's own incentive programmes.

The key is to approach renewal 90–120 days in advance, with a clean licence position analysis and a clear sense of your alternatives. Microsoft's commercial teams respond to preparation and competition — customers who arrive at renewal without either rarely achieve optimal outcomes.

title: Retail: Zero-Downtime AWS Migration
desc: Moving a legacy monolithic application to microservices on AWS.
author: Daniel Park
keyTakeaways: Zero minutes of customer-facing downtime across the full migration programme
42% reduction in infrastructure costs post-migration
Deployment frequency increased from monthly releases to multiple per day
Migration completed 3 weeks ahead of schedule despite peak trading season

sections.heading: Client Background
body: Our client is a leading omnichannel retailer with 200+ stores across Southeast Asia and a rapidly growing e-commerce operation. Their core e-commerce platform had been running on a legacy Java monolith since 2011 — a system that had served them well in a simpler era but was now a serious constraint on growth.

Peak trading events — including regional shopping festivals that drive 5–8× normal transaction volumes — were requiring the engineering team to provision dedicated hardware weeks in advance and run manual scaling playbooks during high-traffic periods. The system could not autoscale, and any deployment required a full overnight maintenance window.

sections.heading: Why Zero Downtime Was Non-Negotiable
body: For a retailer of this scale, downtime is not merely an inconvenience — it is directly quantifiable. The client's finance team had calculated that a one-hour outage during a peak trading day costs approximately $1.2M in lost revenue and an additional $400K in customer service costs.

The business had experienced two significant outages in the 18 months prior to the engagement, both linked to deployment failures. Leadership was unwilling to accept any migration approach that introduced additional downtime risk. This became the non-negotiable constraint around which our entire architecture and migration sequencing was designed.

sections.heading: The Migration Approach
body: Cloudyo selected the Strangler Fig pattern as the primary migration strategy — incrementally extracting services from the monolith and routing traffic to new microservices via an API gateway, while the legacy system continued to serve requests in parallel. This approach eliminates the need for a cutover and allows individual services to be migrated, tested, and rolled back independently.

The migration was sequenced by domain: product catalogue and search first (low write contention, high read traffic — ideal for demonstrating scale benefits), followed by cart and checkout, then order management, and finally authentication and customer profiles. Each domain extraction was preceded by a comprehensive contract testing phase to ensure API compatibility.

sections.heading: AWS Architecture and Tooling
body: The target architecture was built on Amazon EKS for container orchestration, with Amazon RDS Aurora replacing the legacy MySQL cluster and Amazon DynamoDB handling session data and product catalogue lookups. AWS Application Load Balancer with weighted target group routing enabled gradual traffic shifting from monolith to microservices at the 1%, 10%, 25%, 50%, and 100% levels.

AWS CodePipeline and CodeDeploy automated the CI/CD pipeline, reducing deployment time from 4 hours (legacy) to 12 minutes. CloudWatch dashboards and alarms provided real-time visibility into service health throughout the migration, with automated rollback triggers configured at key traffic thresholds.

sections.heading: Results
body: The full migration programme was completed over 7 months — three weeks ahead of the original plan. Zero minutes of customer-facing downtime were recorded across the entire engagement, including during the client's annual mid-year sale event, which fell midway through the migration.

Post-migration infrastructure costs fell by 42% versus the pre-migration on-premises and legacy cloud spend, driven by autoscaling efficiency, Reserved Instance coverage, and the elimination of over-provisioned capacity that had been maintained as a safety margin. Deployment frequency increased from one major release per month to an average of four per day.

title: The State of Software Asset Management
desc: Industry benchmark data on software utilisation and waste.
author: Priya Sharma
keyTakeaways: Average enterprise wastes 34% of software licence spend on unused or underused assets
Only 28% of organisations have a mature SAM programme in place
Publisher audits are increasing in frequency — Oracle, Microsoft, and IBM lead in volume
Cloud and SaaS proliferation has made traditional SAM approaches insufficient

sections.heading: About This Report
body: This report draws on Cloudyo's analysis of software estates across 140 enterprise engagements conducted between January 2023 and June 2024, spanning financial services, retail, manufacturing, and public sector organisations in Asia Pacific and EMEA.

Collectively, these organisations manage over $4.2B in annual software spend. The patterns we observe across this dataset provide a uniquely detailed picture of how enterprises are managing — and mismanaging — their software assets in an increasingly complex licensing landscape.

sections.heading: Key Finding: The Waste Problem
body: Across all engagements, the average organisation was wasting 34% of its software licence budget on assets that were either entirely unused, assigned to departed employees, or deployed at a higher tier than required for the actual usage pattern.

This waste is not evenly distributed. The highest-waste categories are productivity suites (primarily Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace), where seat creep and over-provisioning of premium tiers are pervasive, and enterprise applications (ERP, CRM, ITSM), where named-user licences are routinely assigned without usage verification.

sections.heading: SAM Maturity Distribution
body: We assessed SAM maturity across five dimensions: discovery coverage, entitlement management, usage monitoring, renewal governance, and audit readiness. Organisations were categorised across four maturity levels:
bullets: Level 1 — Reactive (39% of respondents): No formal SAM programme. Licence data lives in spreadsheets. Audits are managed reactively and expensively.
Level 2 — Aware (33% of respondents): Basic discovery tooling in place. Renewal calendar exists but renewal strategy is limited to renewing what was purchased previously.
Level 3 — Managed (20% of respondents): Dedicated SAM capability, integrated tooling, regular compliance reviews, and proactive renewal management.
Level 4 — Optimised (8% of respondents): SAM is embedded in IT governance. Continuous compliance posture, cloud and SaaS visibility, and commercial intelligence used in every vendor negotiation.

sections.heading: The Audit Landscape
body: Software publisher audits increased by 23% year-on-year in the period covered by this report. Oracle remains the most aggressive auditor by volume, followed by Microsoft (particularly in the context of NCE transitions) and IBM. The average cost of a reactive audit response — including legal fees, compliance project costs, and settlement — was $2.1M for organisations with >1,000 employees.

Organisations at SAM Maturity Level 3 and above experienced significantly lower audit exposure: 78% were able to demonstrate a clean licence position within 30 days of an audit notification, versus 12% at Level 1. The investment in proactive SAM pays for itself many times over in audit risk reduction alone.

sections.heading: Cloud and SaaS: The New SAM Frontier
body: Traditional SAM programmes were designed for on-premises perpetual licences. The shift to cloud subscription and SaaS has fundamentally changed the SAM challenge — and exposed the limitations of legacy tooling and processes.

SaaS applications are typically procured outside of central IT (shadow IT), creating an unmanaged sprawl of active subscriptions, redundant tools, and orphaned accounts. Cloudyo's data shows the average enterprise has 4.2× more active SaaS subscriptions than their IT department is aware of. A modern SAM programme must extend to SaaS discovery, contract consolidation, and usage-based optimisation.

sections.heading: Recommendations
body: Based on our benchmark data, we recommend the following priority actions regardless of current SAM maturity:
bullets: Conduct a full software estate discovery using automated tooling, not manual surveys. You cannot manage what you cannot see.
Establish a renewal calendar with 90-day advance notice for all contracts above $50,000. Reactive renewals consistently result in worse commercial outcomes.
Implement a leavers process that triggers licence reclamation within 48 hours of employee departure. Departed employee licences represent 11% of total waste in our dataset.
Extend SAM coverage to SaaS by integrating an identity provider (Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace) with a SaaS management platform to gain visibility into active applications and usage.
Engage independent advisors before any major publisher audit. The cost of preparation is a fraction of the cost of an unprepared settlement.
